Let \(m=(p-1)/2=2t+1\), which is odd.

Suppose first that \(a\) is a primitive root modulo \(p\). Then \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=p-1=2m\). Hence \(a^m\) has order \(2\), so \(a^m\equiv-1\pmod p\). Therefore
\[
(-a)^m=(-1)^m a^m\equiv(-1)(-1)\equiv1\pmod p.
\]
Thus \(\operatorname{ord}_p(-a)\mid m\). Conversely, if \((-a)^n\equiv1\pmod p\), then
\[
a^{2n}=(-a)^{2n}\equiv1\pmod p.
\]
Since \(a\) has order \(2m\), this implies \(2m\mid2n\), hence \(m\mid n\). Consequently \(\operatorname{ord}_p(-a)=m=(p-1)/2\).

Conversely, suppose \(\operatorname{ord}_p(-a)=m\). Put \(x=-a\). Since \(m\) is odd, \(x\) has odd order \(m\), while \(-1\) has order \(2\). These two orders are coprime. Because \(a=-x\), the commuting elements \(-1\) and \(x\) have product of order
\[
\operatorname{lcm}(2,m)=2m=p-1.
\]
Thus \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=p-1\), so \(a\) is a primitive root modulo \(p\).

feedback.reason: The proof correctly handles both implications. It uses that m=(p-1)/2 is odd, the unique element of order 2 modulo an odd prime is -1, and commuting elements of coprime orders 2 and m have product of order 2m. All required conclusions follow.

problem.proof_text:
\begin{proof}

    Let $a$ a primitive root modulo $p$.

As $a^{p-1} \equiv 1(\bmod p), p \mid\left(a^{(p-1) / 2}-1\right)\left(a^{(p-1) / 2}+1\right)$, so $p \mid a^{(p-1) / 2}-1$ or $p \mid$ $a^{(p-1) / 2}+1$. As $a$ is a primitive root modulo $p, a^{(p-1) / 2} \not \equiv 1(\bmod p)$, so

$$

a^{(p-1) / 2} \equiv-1 \quad(\bmod p) .

$$

Hence $(-a)^{(p-1) / 2}=(-1)^{2 t+1} a^{(p-1) / 2} \equiv(-1) \times(-1)=1(\bmod p)$.

Suppose that $(-a)^n \equiv 1(\bmod p)$, with $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Then $a^{2 n}=(-a)^{2 n} \equiv 1(\bmod p)$, so $p-1\left|2 n, \frac{p-1}{2}\right| n$.

So $-a$ has order $(p-1) / 2$ modulo $p$.

Conversely, suppose that $-a$ has order $(p-1) / 2=2 t+1$ modulo $p$. Let $2, p_1, \ldots p_k$ the prime factors of $p-1$, where $p_i$ are odd.

$a^{(p-1) / 2}=a^{2 t+1}=-(-a)^{2 t+1}=-(-a)^{(p-1) / 2} \equiv-1$, so $a^{(p-1) / 2} \not \equiv 1(\bmod 2)$.

As $p-1$ is even, $(p-1) / p_i$ is even, so $a^{(p-1) / p_i}=(-a)^{(p-1) / p_i} \not \equiv 1(\bmod p)($ since $-a$ has order $p-1)$.

So the order of $a$ is $p-1$ (see Ex. 4.8) : $a$ is a primitive root modulo $p$.

\end{proof}
problem.theorem: Consider a prime $p$ of the form $4 t+3$. Show that $a$ is a primitive root modulo $p$ iff $-a$ has order $(p-1) / 2$.
